s3_subtitle: From a humble Stuttgart workshop to global industry leader for piano actions and hammerheads
s3_notes: Slide 3: Timeline of 140+ years of tradition (9 milestones). Key focus on Milestone 1 (1882: Founding in Stuttgart – The journey begins with piano actions; parallel to Carl Rönisch), Milestone 2 (1906: Dedicated hammerhead manufacturing – From Cristofori's leather-covered paper roll in 1700 to Renner's proprietary hammerhead production from 1906, which would later define the tone of every Steinway grand and establish a worldwide benchmark; image series featuring Cristofori, 1700 hammer action, historical action manufacturing and 1906 hammerhead presses), Milestone 3 (1911: Modernization & grand action manufacturing – Érard repetition action as cornerstone of modern grand piano playing; transition to Renner's first grand piano actions; Oscar Renner's industrial modernization with cutting-edge machinery, streamlined methods and transition from shaft drives to hundreds of individual electric motors; uniting all branches under one roof; image series featuring Sébastien Érard, 1808 Érard action and electrified workshop), Milestone 4 (1944: Air raid & rebuilding), Milestone 5 (1951/1952: Dr. Manfred Renner; 1955 return), Milestone 6 (1990: Fall of the Wall, historic turning point & survival – acquisition of Piano Union's action facility in Zeitz amidst pressure from Czech competitors to preserve largest customer Schimmel producing >40 pianos/day), Milestone 7 (2011: New facility in Gärtringen and modern manufacturing in Meuselwitz after relocating from Zeitz; consolidation across two core sites: Meuselwitz 6,800 m² and Gärtringen; image series featuring Gärtringen new facility and Meuselwitz bird's-eye view), Milestone 8 (2019: Steinway & Sons acquisition; tribute to Clemens von Arnim) and Milestone 9 (Preserving tradition, shaping future: Full consolidation of all operations in Meuselwitz following October 2025 launch with modern facility and new central filtration & extraction system; gratitude to Gärtringen workforce).

s5_title: Filzfabrik Wurzen (FFW) – The Birthplace of Piano Hammer Felt
s5_subtitle: Since 1783 • From the first German piano felt in 1847 to the renaissance of “Weickert Spezial” for Renner
s5_m1_subtitle: The historic roots in Leipzig of the world's oldest industrial felt manufactory
s5_m1_bullet_1: Leipzig Workshop: In 1783, Johann Dankegott Weickert laid the cornerstone in Leipzig with a specialized workshop for optical instruments and fine woolen goods.
s5_m1_bullet_2: Wholesale Expansion: Son August Moritz Weickert expanded the firm into a major wholesale house for precision tools and quality materials.
s5_m1_bullet_3: Birth of the Fortepiano: As the hammer-action piano evolved in the late 18th century, piano makers began searching for the ideal striking medium.
s5_m1_caption: From hand-carded raw wool fleece to ultra-dense Weickert felt blocks
s5_m2_title: Germany's First Viable Piano Hammer Felt
s5_m2_subtitle: Friedrich Wilhelm & Carl Wilhelm Patzschke revolutionize piano manufacturing
s5_m2_bullet_1: Felt Replaces Leather: In 1847, Leipzig wool merchants F.W. and C.W. Patzschke succeeded in producing a dense felt that replaced uneven leather hammer coverings.
s5_m2_bullet_2: Weickert Partnership: August Moritz Weickert financed large-scale industrialization; Carl Wilhelm Patzschke served as technical manufacturing director.
s5_m2_bullet_3: Quest for Pure Water: Initial trials in Werdau proved that pure white piano felt requires perfectly clean river water and soot-free air.
s5_m2_caption: Golzernmühle near Grimma (1850): Early felt making on an island in the Mulde river
s5_m3_title: World Expos & Gold Medals in London & Paris
s5_m3_subtitle: International triumphs, royal visits, and worldwide critical acclaim
s5_m3_bullet_1: Prestigious Awards: Medals at the 1850 Leipzig Industrial Expo, the 1851 Great Exhibition in London, and the 1867 Paris World's Fair cemented global fame.
s5_m3_bullet_2: Royal Visits: The Kings of Saxony personally toured the manufacturing halls, honoring the outstanding quality of Saxon piano felt.
s5_m3_bullet_3: Purveyor to Elite Makers: Master piano builders in Vienna, Paris, and London rapidly switched exclusively to resilient Weickert felt.
s5_m3_caption: Historical World Expo medals awarded for superlative felt excellence
s5_m4_title: Relocation to Wurzen: Steam Power & Pure Mulde Water
s5_m4_subtitle: Erection of the state-of-the-art piano felt manufactory at Mühlgraben Wurzen
s5_m4_bullet_1: Mühlgraben Facility: In 1861, the company relocated to Wurzen, constructing sprawling production halls and a central steam engine boiler house.
s5_m4_bullet_2: Steam-Driven Fulling Mills: Custom-engineered fulling and felting machines achieved unprecedented elasticity, density, and batch consistency.
s5_m4_bullet_3: The Mulde River Secret: The soft, mineral-poor river water proved to be the ultimate natural asset for gentle, residue-free wool scouring.
s5_m4_fact: ⚙️ Steam fulling & pure soft Mulde river water
s5_m4_caption: Original historical engraving of Pianofortefilzfabrik in Wurzen (1871)
s5_m5_title: Global Market Leader for 200,000 Pianos Annually
s5_m5_subtitle: Purveyor to Steinway New York, Patzschke Villa & 350 craftsmen
s5_m5_bullet_1: Felt for 200,000 Pianos: At its peak in 1903, Wurzen produced hammer felt for approximately 200,000 grand and upright pianos every year.
s5_m5_bullet_2: Global Export Giant: Foremost customer was Steinway & Sons New York, alongside premier makers in France, England, Russia, and Italy.
s5_m5_bullet_3: Patzschke Dynasty: Inside the 1883/84 Patzschke Villa on site, three generations directed 350 skilled felt masters.
s5_m5_caption: Villa Patzschke on factory grounds – Residence and headquarters across 3 generations
s5_m6_subtitle: Reprivatization by the Brand family & exclusive gold standard for Louis Renner
s5_m6_bullet_1: 1991 Reprivatization: The Brand family reprivatized the facility alongside Weickert heirs; piano builders worldwide demanded the return of the authentic formula.
s5_m6_bullet_2: Rebirth of Weickert Spezial: In 2010, reintroducing the legendary Weickert Spezial formula brought full circle the peak standard of 1903.
s5_m6_bullet_3: Exclusive Renner Symbiosis: Today Louis Renner sources its entire premium hammerhead felt from Wurzen for unparalleled acoustic clarity and power.
s5_m6_caption: Wurzen Weickert Spezial felt: Flawless voicing response & tonal depth
s5_felt_title: The Acoustic Secret of Weickert Felt
s5_felt_subtitle: Pure mechanical fulling without chemical binders – the irreplaceable acoustic soul of the concert grand
s5_hl1_desc: Pure natural virgin fibers with microscopic scales that physically lock together during humid mechanical fulling.
s5_hl2_desc: Densified exclusively by hot river water, friction, and pressure – zero acoustic damping caused by hardened glues.
s5_hl3_desc: Organic keratin elasticity snaps back in milliseconds from the string, preventing energy loss and muting.
s5_hl4_desc: Only strictly hand-selected Wurzen Weickert Spezial sheets meet Renner's exacting acoustic tolerances.
s5_notes: Slide 5: The company history of Filzfabrik Wurzen (FFW) from 1783 to the present and the acoustic secret of Weickert felt. Introduce the 6 historical milestones: 1783 founding in Leipzig by J.D. Weickert, 1847 invention of the first German piano hammer felt by the Patzschke family (replacing leather hammer covers), 1850-1867 London & Paris World Expos with royal honors, 1861 relocation to Wurzen with steam engines and soft Mulde river water, 1903 world leader for 200,000 pianos annually (Steinway New York), and 2010 the renaissance of 'Weickert Spezial' exclusively for Louis Renner. On the right side, highlight the premium felt: 100% pure Merino virgin wool, purely mechanical fulling without resins or binders, permanent elastic springback, and its critical role in shaping the singing European grand piano tone.

s7_title: Pure Virgin Wool: Preserving Natural Fiber Elasticity
s7_subtitle: Only uncompressed raw wool guarantees maximum natural elasticity
s7_bullet_1: Bale Delivery Without Over-Compression: Raw wool is transported in loosely packed bales. Excessive compression would irreversibly damage the delicate scales and crimp of the wool fibers.
s7_bullet_2: Higher Logistics Costs for Supreme Quality: This gentle handling increases transport volume, but safeguards intact fiber elasticity.
s7_bullet_3: Pronounced Fiber Crimp: Only highly crimped Merino wool fibers provide optimal interlocking during the subsequent fulling process.
s7_bullet_4: Gentle Carbonization: A chemically gentle cleansing process removes plant matter without attacking the keratin protein structure.
s7_caption_1: Raw wool delivery: Gently stored wool bales at FFW
s7_notes: Slide 7: Present the key highlights and emphasize Louis Renner's German precision craftsmanship.
s8_subtitle: Loosening and blending distinct wool batches for tailor-made densities
s8_bullet_1: Blending Process: Mixing different fiber lengths and finenesses to achieve specific spring stiffness and resilience.
s8_bullet_2: Fiber Loosening: Multi-stage mechanical picking and aeration gently separate fiber clumps into individual filaments.
s8_bullet_3: Climate Conditioning: Constant moisture absorption prior to carding prevents electrostatic charging and fiber breakage.

s9_title: Carding: Parallel Alignment into Flowing Fleece
s9_subtitle: Defined fiber orientation as the foundation for resonance and string response
s9_bullet_1: Carding: Loosened fibers are combed through fine wire rollers, untangled, and arranged in parallel alignment.
s9_bullet_2: Defined Fiber Direction: The resulting gossamer-thin, soft web features a precisely specified preferential fiber orientation.
s9_bullet_3: Layering: Multiple web layers are superimposed in cross-lap and longitudinal arrangements to build the required sheet thickness and density gradient.
s9_bullet_4: Prerequisite for Voicing: Only parallel-aligned fibers react predictably and evenly to voicing needle penetration during subsequent tone regulation.
s9_caption_1: Carding wool into silky flowing webs with defined fiber orientation

s10_title: The 4 Pillars of Fulling: Steam, Pressure, Motion & Know-How
s10_subtitle: Fiber entanglement through natural physical-thermal stimulation
s10_c1_desc: Opens the microscopic cuticle scales of the hair filaments and renders keratin supple.
s10_c2_desc: Continuously compresses the fleece layers, initiating progressive density increase.
s10_c3_desc: Frictional rubbing interlocks the natural barbed scales of fibers inextricably.
s10_c4_desc: Sensory feel for the exact moment of completion governs elasticity and acoustic resonance.

s11_title: 0.56 Shore: Limit of Natural Fulling Hardness
s11_subtitle: Maximum natural elasticity by eliminating chemical or thermal hardening
s11_c1_desc: During fulling, felt sheets are compacted until fibers cannot be compressed further by purely mechanical means. This corresponds to the maximum natural fulling hardness of approx. 0.56 Shore.

s12_title: Cold Setting with Felt Hammers & Finishing Stones
s12_subtitle: Final dimensional calibration without sanding – preserving the silky fiber cuticle
s12_bullet_1: Mechanical Hammering: Specialized felt hammers and polished natural stones consolidate sheets to exact target dimensions.
s12_bullet_2: Zero Sanding: Sanding felt shears off millions of natural fibers. The Weickert process completely eliminates surface grinding or sanding.
s12_bullet_3: Smooth Bending Radius: When wrapped around the hammer moulding, the felt surface remains completely intact and smooth without split cracking.

s41_title: Calculating Boring Length without Existing Samples
s41_subtitle: The proven 4-step calculation method developed by Renner Academy
s41_caption_1: Measurement diagram for determining hammer boring depth in grands
s41_bullet_1: 1. Blow Distance & Key Dip: Measure action blow distance (46–48 mm) and key dip (10–10.5 mm) precisely.
s41_bullet_2: 2. Flange Rail Reference: Use height of flange rail relative to string underside as datum plane.
s41_bullet_3: 3. Apply Rule of Thumb: Boring length = overall length - 24 mm for standard grand piano geometries.
s41_bullet_4: 4. Mathematical Verification: Ensure a shank protrusion of at least 3 mm for structural integrity.

s43_subtitle: Pre-assembly in field sections according to piano scale division
s43_bullet_1: Distribution in Sections: Mount shanks in sections according to string division, leaving 1-2 positions open between sections.
s43_bullet_2: Starting in the Treble: Begin from note 88 working down toward bass, following Renner's factory packaging order.
s43_bullet_3: Left-Hand Thread Catch: On used action rails, turn the screw counter-clockwise first until it drops into the existing thread pitch, then tighten lightly.
s43_bullet_4: New Screws with Disc Springs: Recommended: Renner screws with spring washers (item no. 43-0008745) for clean seating.

s44_subtitle: Acoustic frequency pairing of shanks to balance string response
s44_bullet_1: Tapping Shanks: Lightly tapping unglued hammer shanks against the rail reveals their acoustic pitch.
s44_bullet_2: Ascending Frequency: Group shanks with ascending resonance frequency from bass to high treble.
s44_bullet_3: Acoustic Uniformity: Prevents isolated 'dead' notes and balances dynamic transmission across section breaks.

s45_title: Traveling: Ensuring Straight Shank Travel with Paper Shims
s45_subtitle: Truing the shank path using blue paper under-spacers (Item 43-0005975)
s45_bullet_1: 90° Alignment of Boundary Shanks: Align the first and last shank of each section strictly perpendicular to the rail.
s45_bullet_2: Traveling Correction: Shanks tracking off-center are corrected by placing 0.2 mm blue gummed paper (item 43-0005975) under the flange.
s45_bullet_3: Angled Felt Knife (Item 43-0003252): Enables clean insertion and trimming of paper shims under the flange base.
s45_bullet_4: Section Shifting: Entire scale sections in older grands can be systematically shifted left or right to align with string spacing.

s46_subtitle: Why key numbers must be freshly applied in pencil prior to gluing
s46_bullet_1: Sorting Out Spares: Lay the set out on the bench and separate extra spare hammers.
s46_bullet_2: Risk of Losing Numbers: Because hammer mouldings are tapered narrower than the cut width, factory markings are frequently planed off!
s46_bullet_3: Re-Numbering in Pencil: All 88 hammerheads must be re-numbered on their underside with soft pencil before gluing begins.

s47_bullet_3: Conical Reaming: The cylindrical factory bore is reamed to match the exact 1:50 taper of the Renner shank.
s47_bullet_4: Checking Friction Fit: The hammerhead must seat firmly and without wobble on the dry shank before adhesive is applied.

s48_title: The Taper Principle: Conical Shank & Conical Hole
s48_subtitle: Why cylindrical bores fail and conical friction locking creates indestructible joints
s48_bullet_1: No Glue Scraping: With cylindrical shanks, sliding the head on pushes glue outward – starving the joint of adhesive.
s48_bullet_2: Even Glue Film: With conical fits, wood surfaces make contact only across the final fraction of a millimeter.
s48_bullet_3: Wood Swelling Creates Wedge Lock: Moisture in the glue swells wood fibers in the bore, locking the shank in an unbreakable friction weld.

s49_bullet_2: Why 91°? The subtle 1° forward pitch exactly compensates for dynamic shank deflection under concert attack loads.
s49_bullet_3: Checking Reference Hammers: The first and last hammer of each section are precisely aligned to the 91° gauge.

s51_bullet_1: Double Glue Application: Thin glue film on the shank tip and dripless application inside the bore.
s51_bullet_2: Rotational Motion: Twist hammerhead ~90° back and forth while seating -> guarantees a continuous 360° glue bead.
s51_bullet_3: Rule of Three: Glue 3 hammers in sequence and immediately sight the center one against reference guide hammers.

s60_title: Pre-Voicing (Pre-Needling): Deep 90° Stitches in Blue Wedge
s60_subtitle: Relieving factory pre-tension and channeling elastic energy into the forte wedge
s60_bullet_1: Work Zone: Exclusively in the blue fortissimo wedge (clock zones 9:00–10:00 and 2:00–3:00).
s60_bullet_2: Deep Needling: Insert needles deeply to just short of the underfelt (never pierce underfelt or core wood!).
s60_bullet_3: Tension Transfer: The head sheds rigid factory stiffness; stored tension flows into the green forte wedge.
s60_bullet_4: Recommendation: This step is recommended almost without exception prior to first playing-in in the instrument.

s61_subtitle: Press, do not chop – Exact stitch counts for bass, mid-range, and treble
s61_bullet_1:
Stitch Counts for Pre-Needling:
• Bass: 7–10 stitches horizontally
• Mid-Range: 5–10 stitches horizontally
• Treble: 0–7 stitches vertically
s61_bullet_2: Press, never chop! Press needles steadily using body weight. Chopping tears wool fibers uncontrollably!

s62_bullet_1: Setting Hitch Pins: Carefully seat strings from back to front at hitch pins using a brass drift punch and light hammer.
s62_bullet_2: Bridge Pin Alignment: Seat strings on the bridge with Renner bridge punch to eliminate false beats.
s62_bullet_3: Unison Purity: Before the first voicing needle, the unison must ring absolutely pure and free of unwanted friction.

s63_subtitle: Optimizing notes 69–88 by micro-shifting the keyframe strike line
s63_bullet_1: Test Strike Point on Note 88: Shift keyframe slightly forward and back to locate the brightest, most singing treble sweet spot.
s63_bullet_2: Optimize Notes 69 to 88: The high treble on many grands improves dramatically once the strike line is precisely repositioned!
s63_bullet_3: Squareness of All Hammers: Test by plucking strings or lifting jacks with finger; mark corrections with chalk on key tops.

s64_c1_desc: Crown contacts only outer strings -> incomplete attack tone, must be filed level.
s64_c2_desc: Asymmetrical contact creates double attack and string buzz -> file true to string plane.
s64_c3_desc: Simultaneous solid contact on all 3 unison strings for a full fundamental tone.

s65_title: Intermediate & Fine Voicing: The 2 mm Limit at the Crown
s65_subtitle: Chromatic listening and delicate evening-out of individual notes
s65_bullet_1: Chromatic Play-Through: Play chromatically up and down the keyboard; flag notes with harsh attack or uneven volume.
s65_bullet_2: Mid-Voicing: Gentle needle pricks in green forte and orange piano wedges. Overly soft notes are firmed by light surface sanding!
s65_bullet_3: Final Voicing: Short single needle (BDK handle item 43-0003269 or Chop Stick item 43-0003271).
s65_bullet_4: Max. 2 mm Depth at Crown: Insert only between string grooves, never directly into the string depressions!
